summary: ICARUS-45 is a digital micro-atmosphere management and life-support simulation concept designed for future Mars research bases and human exploration missions. The project aims to model controlled atmospheric environments around research capsules by analyzing nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), and argon (Ar) compositions under different temperature and pressure conditions. Using publicly available NASA Mars research data, ICARUS-45 aims to analyze environmental conditions and simulate alternative atmospheric scenarios. Its modular architecture consists of four main components: Mars Environment, Atmosphere Lab, ICARUS Control, and Mission Report. The project addresses the challenges of Mars' low atmospheric pressure and high carbon dioxide concentration by exploring how localized atmospheric environments could be modeled and evaluated. ICARUS-45 aims to support future planetary research by providing an adaptable digital framework for studying atmospheric conditions and life-support concepts.
details:
ICARUS-45 is a digital simulation framework that explores how controlled micro-atmospheres could be modeled around future Mars research bases. It uses publicly available NASA Mars environmental data (atmospheric pressure, temperature, carbon dioxide concentration) and combines it with selected gas compositions such as nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), and argon (Ar). The system has four components: Mars Environment (NASA data analysis), Atmosphere Lab (gas mixture scenarios), ICARUS Control (comparing temperature, pressure, composition, and stability), and Mission Report (graphs, comparisons, and reports).
Benefits and intended impact: Mars's natural atmosphere is thin, CO₂-dominated, and subject to extreme temperature swings, so it cannot support human habitation on its own. ICARUS-45 gives researchers a low-cost, risk-free way to test and compare alternative atmospheric scenarios digitally before any physical hardware is built. Our goal is to provide a foundation for future research into Mars habitats and life-support technologies, and to make NASA's open planetary data easier to explore.
Tools and technologies: Python for data processing and simulation models, NASA Open Data sources (Mars Climate Database, InSight, Planetary Data System, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter), data visualization for graphs and scenario comparisons, and a planned digital control panel for exploring results. No physical hardware is used at this stage.
Creativity: Instead of treating Mars as a whole, we focus on the localized micro-atmosphere around a single capsule or base, and turn raw planetary data into an interactive scenario-comparison tool.
Factors considered: scientific reliability of the data sources, the harsh Martian conditions (low pressure, CO₂, temperature swings, dust, radiation), and clarity of results. ICARUS-45 is a proposed simulation framework, not a physical life-support system. Future goals include more complex simulations, sensor integration, atmospheric monitoring, and life-support research.
